protocol.instrument_name: Acute Nausea and Vomiting Associated with Gastroenteritis – Clinical Practice Guideline
protocol.legal_basis: Authorisation page (p2): 'Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative. In accordance with regulation 17A of the Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 2011 (the Poisons Regulations) a pharmacist is authorised to prescribe a prescription drug (not being a drug of dependence) if the pharmacist is included on the register of authorised pharmacists and the drug is prescribed in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code.'
protocol.supervision_model: Document does not use 'collaborative'/'autonomous' terminology; its own wording: an authorised pharmacist on the register of authorised pharmacists prescribing in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code (p2). Discretion clause (p6): 'When applying the information contained within this clinical practice guideline, pharmacists are advised to exercise professional discretion and judgement. The clinical practice guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual, in consultation with the patient and/or their carer.' Schedule 3 supply notes for prochlorperazine and promethazine are printed at p8 (NB1, NB2).
protocol.scope_summary: SA Health (Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative) clinical practice guideline for pharmacist assessment and management of acute nausea and vomiting associated with gastroenteritis. Service restricted to patients aged 18 years or over. Covers 'Red flag' warning signs necessitating referral to emergency medical care (immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000; urgent referral to an emergency department – patient may make their own way; urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours to a general practitioner), 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' situations, key points, patient history, examination (including abdominal guarding), a non-exhaustive differential list of possible causes (Appendix 1 with per-condition actions), management (supportive oral rehydration therapy plus an oral antiemetic per Therapeutic Guidelines, with Schedule 3 pack-size notes for prochlorperazine and promethazine), confirmation of management, communication of the agreed management plan, clinical review and resources. 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

diagnosis_pathways.name: Assessment and management of acute nausea and vomiting associated with gastroenteritis

steps.description: Gather information and assess patient's needs: 'The assessment approach focuses on identifying the cause (or excluding significant underlying diseases) with a view to expectant management or directing specific treatment.' Patient history: 'Sufficient information should be obtained from the patient to identify the likely cause of the nausea/vomiting, and assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines.' The patient history should consider: age; pregnancy and breastfeeding status (if applicable); nature, severity and frequency of symptoms; food and/or drink consumed in the last 24 hours; onset and duration of symptoms, including timing in relation to eating/drinking; recent head trauma or injury; similar symptoms in close contacts; exposure to toxins, poisons, bites or stings; recent travel; other symptoms e.g., chest pain or heartburn, headache, dizziness, fever, abdominal pain, last bowel motion, diarrhoea, constipation, dysuria, or frequency of urination; precipitating and relieving factors; underlying medical conditions e.g., diabetes or recent surgery; current medications (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements, and over-the-counter medicines), including initiation of new medicines; medication tried to treat current symptoms; alcohol and drug history, including recent illicit drug or alcohol use; mental health history. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients: 'Consider referring to the CARPA Standard Treatment Manual for further information for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients living in rural and remote communities (10).' Reminder: 'Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies and current medical conditions.' Key points (p5): 'It is essential to consider the clinical context when assessing patients with nausea and vomiting, including the possibility of life-threatening causes, before developing an individualised management plan (5, 7).' 'Causes of nausea and vomiting can stem from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, the central nervous system (CNS), or result from a systemic condition, and can often be attributed to an identifiable cause, most commonly acute gastroenteritis, food poisoning or other toxins, migraine, cannabis use, motion sickness or pregnancy (2, 7).'

gates.criterion: Sufficient information obtained to identify the likely cause of the nausea/vomiting and to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines

pregnancy and breastfeeding status (if applicable) assessed — 'The patient is pregnant' is a treat-and-concurrently-refer situation (EXC-23 / RF-24); pregnancy is also an Appendix 1 cause requiring referral
recent head trauma or injury assessed — 'History of head injury / trauma' requires urgent referral to an emergency department (EXC-9 / RF-10)
underlying medical conditions assessed, including diabetes — 'The patient has diabetes or is immunocompromised' requires urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours (EXC-15 / RF-16)
recent travel assessed — 'The patient has recently returned from overseas' requires urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours (EXC-16 / RF-17)

current medicines and initiation of new medicines assessed — 'The nausea and vomiting are post-operative, chemotherapy/radiation-induced or suspected to be drug-induced' requires urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours (EXC-17 / RF-18)

steps.description: Examination: 'Conduct assessment of vital signs – temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, hydration status.' 'Assess hydration status as per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal (Acute gastroenteritis - Assessment of acute gastroenteritis) (11).' 'Examine for abdominal tenderness or distention, guarding, particularly areas where hernias commonly present, excluding the groin. Abdominal guarding indicates intra-abdominal pathology, e.g., acute abdomen and should be referred urgently to ED – either 000 if vital signs abnormal, or via private vehicle if vital signs normal.'

steps.description: Consider possible causes of nausea and vomiting: 'A non-exhaustive list of possible causes of acute nausea and vomiting are presented in Appendix 1.' 'When in doubt of the cause of the nausea and vomiting, the pharmacist should refer the patient to a medical practitioner.' Appendix 1 (p10-p13) lists causes under Gastrointestinal disorders (adynamic ileus; bowel obstruction; gastroenteritis - viral or bacterial/ food poisoning; gastroparesis; hepatitis; peritonitis or other acute abdominal condition e.g., pancreatitis, appendicitis; toxic ingestion including alcohol), Central nervous system disorders (cannabis use/cannabis hyperemesis syndrome; closed head injury or concussion; CNS haemorrhage; CNS infection e.g., meningitis; increased intracranial pressure; labyrinthitis; migraine; motion sickness), Systemic conditions (advanced cancer, chemotherapy or radiation exposure; diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); drug adverse effect or toxicity; liver or renal failure; severe pain; Addisonian (acute adrenal) crisis) and Other causes (pregnancy; urinary tract infection; SARS-COV-2 infection), each with 'Presentation and suggestive findings' and an 'Action'. In-scope row verbatim: 'Gastroenteritis - viral or bacterial/ food poisoning — Vomiting accompanied by diarrhoea; Normal abdomen when examined; Food poisoning apparent based on history — Self-limiting – May be managed under this guideline.' Standard-pharmacy-treatment rows: 'Migraine — Standard pharmacy treatment and referral to a medical practitioner'; 'Motion sickness — Standard pharmacy treatment'.

gates.criterion: cause of the nausea and vomiting is not in doubt — 'When in doubt of the cause of the nausea and vomiting, the pharmacist should refer the patient to a medical practitioner' (EXC-25 / RF-30)
presentation is consistent with gastroenteritis/food poisoning (vomiting accompanied by diarrhoea, normal abdomen when examined) — 'May be managed under this guideline' (INC-3 / EXE-3)

possibility of life-threatening causes considered before developing an individualised management plan (5, 7)

steps.description: Red-flag triage: ''Red flag' warning signs at patient presentation that necessitate referral to emergency medical care' (p4-p5). (a) 'Immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000:' Patient looks very unwell / very drowsy; Severe headache, altered or loss of consciousness; Fever, rash, neck stiffness, confusion; Symptoms of vertigo; Chest pain, shortness of breath; Blood / 'coffee ground' vomit. (b) 'Urgent referral to an emergency department – patient may make their own way to the emergency department:' Prolonged vomiting (longer than 24 to 48 hours); Rectal bleeding; History of head injury / trauma; Increased blood glucose levels; Abdominal distension or tenderness; Green, bile vomit; Significant recent weight loss; Isolated vomiting, lack of nausea (nausea without vomiting is not uncommon). (c) 'Refer to a general practitioner (or other medical practitioner where appropriate): Urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours:' The patient has diabetes or is immunocompromised; The patient has recently returned from overseas; The nausea and vomiting are post-operative, chemotherapy/radiation-induced or suspected to be drug-induced; Intramuscular administration of an antiemetic is indicated; The nausea and vomiting is chronic (defined by 4 weeks or more of symptoms) (4); The patient has recurring episodes of acute nausea and vomiting; The symptoms have not resolved within 24-48 hours of first commencing (consider earlier referral for elderly patients or patients on concurrent medications that may increase risk of electrolyte disturbances, dehydration); The patient's condition and/or symptoms worsen. (d) 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer ... The patient is pregnant.' (e) Examination: abdominal guarding → 'referred urgently to ED – either 000 if vital signs abnormal, or via private vehicle if vital signs normal'. (f) 'When in doubt of the cause of the nausea and vomiting, the pharmacist should refer the patient to a medical practitioner.' (g) Appendix 1 per-condition Actions (RF-31 to RF-53). See RF-1 to RF-53.

gates.criterion: no 'Immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000' trigger present (EXC-1 to EXC-6 / RF-2 to RF-7; abdominal guarding with abnormal vital signs RF-27; Appendix 1 call-000 rows RF-40 to RF-43, RF-46, RF-47, RF-49, RF-51, RF-52)

steps.description: Management and treatment plan: 'Before starting treatment, it is important to identify, treat or remove the cause of the nausea and vomiting, and ensure adequate hydration (12).' 'Pharmacist management of acute nausea and vomiting includes: supportive management for gastroenteritis: Including oral rehydration therapy to prevent or correct dehydration, in accordance with the Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal (Acute gastroenteritis – Rehydration for acute gastroenteritis in adults) (11). pharmacotherapy: An oral medicine for the treatment of acute nausea and vomiting associated with gastroenteritis mentioned in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal: Nausea and vomiting (Antiemetic drugs in adults) (13).' NB1: 'Prochlorperazine is available as a Schedule 3 medicine limited to a pack size of 10 tablets (5 mg). If there is a need for further medication, the patient should be referred to a medical practitioner.' NB2: 'Promethazine is available as a Schedule 3 in a pack size of 25 or 50 tablets (25 mg).' Key point (p6): 'An oral antiemetic may be considered for symptom relief if the nausea and vomiting is suspected to be caused by gastroenteritis, although spontaneous improvement of acute nausea and vomiting is likely (7).' Confirm management is appropriate (p8): 'Pharmacists must consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references to confirm that the treatment recommendation is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and breastfeeding.'

provenance.section_heading: Management and treatment plan

steps.description: Communicate agreed management plan [heading printed as 'Communiate agreed management plan']: 'Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) as per the Australian Medicines Handbook and other relevant references, should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use e.g., dosing and frequency; supportive care, including the importance of rehydration; how to manage adverse effects; the impact of vomiting on the absorption and effectiveness of other regular medications; when to seek further care and/or treatment, including recognising 'red flags' and dehydration.' 'It is the pharmacist's responsibility to ensure the suitability and accuracy of any resources and information provided to patients (and parents/caregivers if applicable) and to ensure compliance with all copyright conditions.' 'The agreed management plan should be shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent.'

gates.criterion: comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) provided: individual product and medicine use e.g. dosing and frequency; supportive care including the importance of rehydration; how to manage adverse effects; the impact of vomiting on the absorption and effectiveness of other regular medications; when to seek further care and/or treatment, including recognising 'red flags' and dehydration

steps.description: Clinical review: 'Clinical review with the pharmacist is generally not required. If the condition does not improve or resolve within 24-48 hours, the patient should be advised to see a medical practitioner for further investigation.' 'Consider earlier referral for patients that may be at an increased risk of dehydration or associated electrolyte abnormalities, such as elderly patients, or those on concurrent medications that may increase risk of electrolyte disturbances. See Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal (Acute gastroenteritis – Assessment of acute gastroenteritis) for risk factors for dehydration and associated electrolyte abnormalities in adults with acute gastroenteritis (11).' Related trigger (p5): 'The symptoms have not resolved within 24-48 hours of first commencing (consider earlier referral for elderly patients or patients on concurrent medications that may increase risk of electrolyte disturbances, dehydration)' requires urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours.

Appendix 1 rows with medical-practitioner actions: adynamic ileus; gastroparesis; hepatitis; cannabis use (cannabis hyperemesis syndrome); labyrinthitis; migraine ('Standard pharmacy treatment and referral to a medical practitioner'); advanced cancer, chemotherapy or radiation exposure; drug adverse effect ('referral to the original prescriber is required'); pregnancy; urinary tract infection ('referral to a medical practitioner or an appropriate pharmacy service is required'); SARS-COV-2 infection ('Usual pharmacy care and referral to an appropriate healthcare provider').

open_questions.topic: No specific antiemetic agent, strength, dose, frequency or duration printed beyond two Schedule 3 pack-size notes
open_questions.observed: 'An oral medicine for the treatment of acute nausea and vomiting associated with gastroenteritis mentioned in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal: Nausea and vomiting (Antiemetic drugs in adults) (13)'; NB1 prochlorperazine 'pack size of 10 tablets (5 mg)'; NB2 promethazine 'pack size of 25 or 50 tablets (25 mg)'.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document names no dose, frequency or duration; inventing them would breach the never-invent rule. TX-2 to TX-4 dose fields are empty (confidence 'medium'/'unclear').

open_questions.topic: '(5 mg)' and '(25 mg)' read as tablet strengths — not stated explicitly
open_questions.observed: NB1: 'limited to a pack size of 10 tablets (5 mg)'; NB2: 'a pack size of 25 or 50 tablets (25 mg)'.
open_questions.why_unclear: The parenthetical strength is attached to the pack-size sentence; strength recorded as printed and flagged for confirmation against the product/PD.

open_questions.topic: Two pack sizes for promethazine; no rule for which to supply
open_questions.observed: 'Promethazine is available as a Schedule 3 in a pack size of 25 or 50 tablets (25 mg).'
open_questions.why_unclear: No selection rule, quantity rationale, dose, frequency, duration or repeats statement is printed.

open_questions.topic: Ambiguous '24 to 48 hour' thresholds (three separate statements)
open_questions.observed: p4 'Prolonged vomiting (longer than 24 to 48 hours)' (urgent ED); p5 'The symptoms have not resolved within 24-48 hours of first commencing' (urgent GP referral); p8 'If the condition does not improve or resolve within 24-48 hours, the patient should be advised to see a medical practitioner'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Each threshold is printed as a range ('24 to 48'), so a single numeric cut-off cannot be transcribed without inventing one; RF-8, RF-22 and RF-26 are structured: null. Both readings (24h and 48h) recorded.

open_questions.topic: 'Increased blood glucose levels' has no threshold
open_questions.observed: p4 urgent-ED trigger: 'Increased blood glucose levels' — no value, unit or context (fasting/random) printed.
open_questions.why_unclear: Vague trigger captured as qualitative with structured: null; the DKA row separately prints 'ketones are 0.6 or higher'.

open_questions.topic: Ketone threshold '0.6 or higher' has no unit or test type
open_questions.observed: Appendix 1 DKA row: 'call 000 – including if ketones are 0.6 or higher'; 'Patients with diabetes should be advised to check their blood glucose levels and test ketones in blood or urine.'
open_questions.why_unclear: Value 0.6 transcribed as printed with empty unit; blood vs urine ketones are not distinguished for the threshold.

open_questions.topic: Criteria combinatorics not explicitly labelled
open_questions.observed: Inclusion uses all_of (INC-1 to INC-5); exclusions are grouped per printed referral tier with any_of (EXC-1 to EXC-6; EXC-7 to EXC-14; EXC-15 to EXC-22; single-item groups EXC-23 to EXC-25); no AND/OR key is printed.
open_questions.why_unclear: Combinatorics derived from the tier structure ('in the following situations', 'necessitate referral'); recorded here per spec rule 4. EXC-7 confidence is 'medium' solely because of the ambiguous 24-48 hour wording.

open_questions.topic: Mapping of the document's own urgency tiers to action/severity
open_questions.observed: 'Immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000' → ESCALATE_000 / critical; 'Urgent referral to an emergency department – patient may make their own way' → REFER_URGENT / critical; 'Urgent referral within 24 to 48 hours' (GP) → REFER_URGENT / high; 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' → REFER / medium; clinical-review advice → REVIEW_GP / medium; Appendix 'Standard pharmacy treatment and referral' → REVIEW_GP / medium.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document prints its own tiers but no numeric severity; mapping recorded so it can be re-checked.

open_questions.topic: Appendix 1 cross-reference 'Other warning signs (see Page 1)' does not resolve within this document
open_questions.observed: Peritonitis/other acute abdominal condition row: 'Other warning signs (see Page 1) may be present'. Page 1 of this PDF is the cover page; the red-flag lists are on pages 4-5.
open_questions.why_unclear: The cross-reference appears to be inherited from the source Queensland document; recorded as printed without reinterpretation.

open_questions.topic: Appendix 1 rows with 'Standard pharmacy treatment' — inside or outside this Service?
open_questions.observed: 'Motion sickness — ... Standard pharmacy treatment.' (no referral printed); 'Migraine — ... Standard pharmacy treatment and referral to a medical practitioner.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The document does not state whether 'standard pharmacy treatment' for these rows is delivered under this Service or as usual pharmacy care; EXE-4 records the motion-sickness exception with confidence 'medium'.

open_questions.topic: Notifiable wording is hedged ('consider notification')
open_questions.observed: 'For suspected food poisoning, consider notification to local public health unit or make a food safety complaint online.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The document says 'consider', not 'must'; notifiable.required set to true to surface the pathway, with the hedged wording preserved verbatim in conditions — confirm whether a hard requirement is intended (see hugh_to_confirm).

open_questions.topic: Who administers an intramuscular antiemetic, and what follows the indication
open_questions.observed: 'Intramuscular administration of an antiemetic is indicated' is an urgent-referral trigger to a general practitioner; the document does not say who administers it or whether the pharmacist may supply for administration elsewhere.
open_questions.why_unclear: Only the referral consequence is printed; RF-19 structured: null.

open_questions.topic: 'Patient looks very unwell / very drowsy' and 'Significant recent weight loss' are judgement prompts
open_questions.observed: Two of the six call-000 triggers and two own-way ED triggers have no objective definition in the document.
open_questions.why_unclear: Captured with structured: null per spec rule 3 (vague wording → qualitative judgement prompt).

open_questions.topic: Gate on_fail values not stated by the document
open_questions.observed: Branch outcomes are not printed for every gate. Used: STOP for call-000 triggers and for hard prerequisites (cause identified/hydration ensured, confirm-management); REFER for the urgent-ED and 24-48 hour tiers and for 'need for further medication'; SEE_PW-1-S4 to route into red-flag triage; SEE_PW-1-S5 for treat-and-concurrently-refer (pregnancy); 'unclear' where the document states no consequence (history sufficiency, under-18 handling, vital signs, hydration assessment, life-threatening-cause consideration, counselling elements, review-not-required).
open_questions.why_unclear: Some branch outcomes are inferred from directive wording rather than printed explicitly.

open_questions.topic: Action for a patient under 18 years not stated
open_questions.observed: 'Service restricted to patients aged 18 years or over' plus the usual ineligibility statement; no referral action is printed for an under-18 presenter.
open_questions.why_unclear: PW-1-S1 age gate on_fail recorded as 'unclear' because the document states no action beyond ineligibility for the prescribing service.

open_questions.topic: Heading and word-level typographical errors in the source
open_questions.observed: 'Communiate agreed management plan' (p8 heading); 'where approriate' (p5); 'Symptoms revolve after stopping cannabis use' (Appendix 1, cannabis row, p11).
open_questions.why_unclear: Transcribed as printed with [as printed]/[sic] markers; intended readings are obvious but were not silently corrected.

open_questions.topic: Pregnancy appears twice with different instructions
open_questions.observed: p5: 'The patient is pregnant' → 'Provide initial treatment and concurrently refer to a general practitioner'; p12 Appendix: pregnancy → 'Referral to a medical practitioner is required. Non-pharmacological therapies may be recommended as standard pharmacist care.'
open_questions.why_unclear: Both recorded as printed (RF-24 and RF-51); the document does not state whether the treat-and-refer pathway overrides the Appendix action or how non-pharmacological therapies interact with it.

open_questions.topic: No supply quantity, pack rule beyond the two Schedule 3 notes, repeats or duration printed
open_questions.observed: Only pack-size limits are printed (10 tablets; 25 or 50 tablets). No repeat, duration or 'quantity until review' statement exists in this guideline.
open_questions.why_unclear: max_quantity/quantity_to_supply recorded only where printed; otherwise empty (see hugh_to_confirm).

open_questions.topic: Causes list is explicitly non-exhaustive
open_questions.observed: 'A non-exhaustive list of possible causes of acute nausea and vomiting are presented in Appendix 1.'
open_questions.why_unclear: Engine must not treat Appendix 1 as a complete differential; 'When in doubt of the cause ... refer' (RF-30) covers unlisted causes.

open_questions.topic: Reference list URL/section identifiers look mismatched in the extraction
open_questions.observed: References 7, 11 and 13 carry long query strings whose topic files (Gastro-oesophageal-reflux-in-adults) do not match their titles; reference 12 'Antiemetics [Internet]. AMH. 2025.' has no URL.
open_questions.why_unclear: Citation strings transcribed as extracted; discrepancies may be extraction artefacts or source errors.
